chunks: What a square wave is and its properties. The question: What is a square wave? What are its properties?
A square wave is a repeating signal that flips between two levels and spends half of each cycle at each.
It matters because the clock signals that keep digital chips in step, and many power and motor controls, are square or rectangular waves.
A square wave also has a hidden side: it is made of many sine waves added together. The sharper its edges, the more high frequencies it needs.
Picture flipping a light switch up and down at a steady rhythm: on for a second, off for a second. Now picture building a sharp-cornered shape out of smooth round pebbles.
A few pebbles give rounded corners, and many small pebbles make the corners sharp. The pebbles are sine waves, and sharp edges need many of them.
The fundamental alone peaks at 1. 27 amps, above the square wave's level. Adding the 3rd and 5th makes the top flatter and the edges steeper.
With 9 terms the edges are nearly vertical but there is still a spike at each corner, the Gibbs overshoot (about 9% of the step) that never goes away as terms are added.
Duty cycle: the fraction of each period the signal is high. A square wave has 50%. Average (DC) value: the mean level over one period.
RMS value: the steady voltage that would heat a resistor by the same amount. Harmonic: a sine wave at a whole-number multiple of the signal's main frequency.
Rise time: how long an edge takes to go from 10% to 90% of the swing.
Take a 0 to 3. 3 volts clock at 100 megahertz. The period is 10 nanoseconds, with 5 nanoseconds high. The average is 1. 65 volts. The RMS is 3. 3 ÷ √2 about 2.
33 volts, because you average the square of the voltage, not the voltage. Its sine content is at 100 megahertz, 300 megahertz, 500 megahertz and so on, only odd multiples.
The peak sizes are 2 times 3. 3 ÷ (nπ), so about 2. 1 volts, 0. 70 volts and 0. 42 volts.
Real edges are not instant: a 1 nanoseconds rise time puts meaningful content out to roughly 0. 35 ÷ 1 nanoseconds = 350 megahertz. That is the whole idea.
"A square wave is a periodic two-level signal that spends half of each period high and half low, so it's a 50% duty rectangular wave.
For 0 to V the average is V over two and the RMS is about 0. 71 volts.
In the frequency domain it has only odd harmonics, falling as one over n, with a fundamental of 4 amps over pi for a plus-minus A wave.
The ideal one has infinite bandwidth because the edges are instant.
Real ones have a finite rise time, which sets how far the harmonics extend and how much ringing and EMI you get."
